# Models {#sec-models}

To describe trajectories of word learning, we must estimate the number of words children understand, say or sign at different ages. Averages (at each age) are insufficient: families and practitioners also want to know ranges -- how much children typically differ at each age. Our target is therefore the distributions of word counts at monthly age intervals, describing both typical counts and the spreads around them.

We already know a good deal about what shape to expect. When children are beginning to learn their first words, counts must sit close to zero, so the distribution starts narrow. Children then learn new words at different rates, so as the typical count rises with age, the differences between children compound and the distribution widens. Counts are also bounded -- a child cannot know fewer than zero words, and a checklist cannot record more words than it contains -- and vocabulary grows gradually, word by word, so we expect the distribution to shift and spread smoothly with age rather than jump. A statistical model lets us state these expectations precisely and combine them with our data to estimate the distributions we are seeking.

This section introduces our statistical approach -- what statistical models can and cannot claim, and how Bayesian inference expresses uncertainty, uses existing knowledge and supports prediction -- and then describes the models we fit.

## Statistical modelling and Bayesian inference

Statistical modelling and inference offer methods for defining mathematical models and fitting them to data to estimate values of interest [@coxPrinciplesStatisticalInference2006; @gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020; @chanStatisticalModelingComputation2025]. They are central to evaluating scientific theories and interpreting data, and can express what a theory means more precisely than words alone [@farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018, chapter 1].

Statistical models do not by themselves explain how the world works, though they can evaluate the predictions of models that do. A regression model reveals statistical relationships between predictors and outcomes, but those relationships acquire their real-world relevance only within an empirical model -- an account of the real-world phenomenon that informs which statistical and process models can test it [@spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @vanoijenBayesianCompendium2024; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018].

The mapping between the two runs both ways: one empirical model admits many statistical models, and one statistical model is consistent with many empirical models. So even when a statistical model fits the observed data well, we cannot be certain its motivating explanation is 'the right one' — another, equally credible, explanation may fit just as well:

> "Many models correspond to the same hypothesis, and many hypotheses correspond to a single model. This makes strict falsification impossible." [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020, page 4]

Developing and evaluating models is therefore continual and iterative: a competing model may explain the data better, and new observations refine existing models, revise theories and motivate new ones [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

### Different approaches

There are different approaches to statistical inference, differing in their philosophical and mathematical foundations and in the conclusions they license [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

Bayesian methods remain uncommon in developmental Down syndrome research, but for the questions this study addresses they offer four notable advantages: (1) probability statements that mean what most people take them to mean; (2) uncertainty expressed as full distributions; (3) a principled way to bring existing knowledge to bear; and (4) direct predictions about individual children [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @bernardoBayesianStatistics2025; @wagenmakersBayesianInferencePsychology2018; @wagenmakersBayesianFrequentistInference2008].

#### Probability as uncertainty

Bayesian inference treats probability as a measure of uncertainty about unknown quantities -- "relative, in part to this ignorance, in part to our knowledge" [@laplaceEssaiPhilosophiqueProbabilites1814] -- so that a number near one marks an event we consider very likely and a number near zero an event we consider very unlikely [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. On a partly cloudy day, "a 50% chance of rain this afternoon" means that, given what we currently know, rain and no rain seem about equally plausible.

Frequentist uncertainty is instead grounded in how an estimation procedure behaves across repeated samples. A confidence interval is not a probability statement about where the true value lies and does not rank some values as more plausible than others [@moreyFallacyPlacingConfidence2016] -- a distinction that is, unfortunately, often misunderstood [@hoekstraRobustMisinterpretationConfidence2014].

#### Estimates as distributions

Bayesian inference begins with a prior distribution -- what we consider plausible before seeing the data. It then uses Bayes' theorem to update the prior distribution with the data to yield a posterior distribution [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. A Bayesian posterior distribution supports direct and intuitive statements such as: "given our model and the data, the typical 36-month-old child with Down syndrome learns about 5 new words per month, with an 89% probability that the median rate lies between 2 and 7."

### Using existing knowledge

A prior encodes what is plausible about each parameter before the current data are analysed. Priors can draw on previous research and the experience of people with relevant expertise, where this is available. A well-grounded prior combined with the data yields estimates that are more stable, and often more precise, than the data alone -- especially valuable when datasets are small or noisy and a substantial evidence base already exists [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020].

The need to specify a prior is sometimes criticised as subjective. However, all statistical analyses rest on assumptions [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. Arguably, Bayesian priors are more explicit and open to scrutiny. A prior "should be chosen, evaluated, and revised just like all of the other components of the model", and we can test directly how sensitive our estimates are to it [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. For this study, priors let us bring existing knowledge of vocabulary development to bear and improve the accuracy of our estimates.

#### Predictions for individual children

From the posterior we can also predict unobserved outcomes. Drawing parameter values from the posterior and simulating a new observation for each draw yields a *posterior predictive distribution* that carries both the randomness in the data and our uncertainty about the parameters [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. This supports statements such as: "given our model and the data, there is an 89% probability that a 36-month-old child with Down syndrome understands between 0 and 142 words" -- directly useful for setting expectations about individual children.

#### Computation

Bayesian inference is centuries old [@bayesLIIEssaySolving1763; @LaplaceMemoireProbabilite; @laplaceTheorieAnalytiqueProbabilites1820]. For a while, the calculations required were prohibitive for all but the simplest models. However, this is no longer the case:

> "...this was solved in 1990 through the introduction of Markov chain Monte Carlo to use computational power rather than brute analytical derivation. We now exist in an era where there are no intellectual or analytical impediments to specifying and estimating Bayesian models." [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]

Today, modern sampling algorithms [@metropolisEquationStateCalculations1953; @hastingsMonteCarloSampling1970; @hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014], are packaged in freely accessible open-source tools such as Stan and PyMC with interfaces to R and Python [@standevelopmentteamStanLanguageReference2026; @abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023]. Bayesian analysis is consequently now used across economics, political science, ecology, biology, neuroscience, medicine, psychology and education research [@gillBayesianModelingInference2020; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @bonBeingBayesian2020s2023; @pfadtMethodologicalMetamorphosisRapid2025].

## The core model

### The outcome: a count of lexical items {#sec-betabinomial}

Parent-reported vocabulary checklists record a subset of the words a child understands, speaks or signs (@sec-data). Every outcome we model is a count: the total number of checklist words reported understood, spoken or signed.

Each checklist item is answered 'yes' or 'no', so a child's score is a count of 'yes' responses out of $N$ words. Our pooled data include multiple forms with varying numbers of items: the DSE checklists together contain 810 words, while other forms contain between roughly 400 and 700 words (@sec-data). Checklists are designed to sample the words children learn most frequently, and shorter forms are typically given to younger children, so for a child well below a form's maximum, the words a shorter form omits are mostly words the child does not yet know — and the count it records is close to the count a longer inventory would have recorded. Consistent with this, where different forms cover the same ages, median counts correspond more closely on the raw scale than as proportions of their own form. We therefore score every count against a single reference inventory of $N = 810$ words, whichever form recorded it, so that every estimate in this report is on the same scale.

This approximation is less accurate for children near the maximum of a shorter form, who may know words their form does not ask about. Such observations are uncommon among the children with Down syndrome.

#### The Beta-Binomial model

Our models describe parent-reported word counts -- understood, spoken or signed. One completion of a checklist (an *administration*) yields up to one count per *outcome* for a child of a given age. Each such count (one child, one age, one outcome) is an *observation*, the unit whose distribution we now describe.

Each model separates two questions: how the probability that a word is reported *changes* with age (the *growth trajectory*) and how observed counts are spread around the expected count that the probability implies (i.e. out of $N = 810$ words, a probability of $0.5$ implies an expected count $W = 405$). For words understood, for example, the model describes the distribution of the count $W_\text{und}$ at each age in months $A$: $P(W_\text{und} \mid A)$.

A count of 'yes' responses out of $N$ items at a given age follows a Binomial distribution when three assumptions hold. The first two assumptions apply *within* an administration: that (a) given the probability of a 'yes', the item responses (words checked) are independent; and that (b) every item carries that same probability. The third assumption applies *across* administrations: that (c) the probability is the same for every observation at the same age. Vocabulary scores vary far more between same-age children than one shared probability allows, and the Binomial cannot absorb the excess -- its variance is fixed by its mean [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013, sec. 17.2]. The Beta-Binomial distribution relaxes (c), and only (c): each observation's probability is itself drawn from a Beta distribution whose mean is the trajectory value at that age, so individual children's scores are distributed above and below the curve, while (a) and (b) continue to hold within each observation.

The Binomial distribution describes the number of 'yes' responses out of a fixed number of items when, given a success probability, (i) the item responses are independent and (ii) every item shares that same probability. Applying a single Binomial across children would add a third assumption: that (iii) every observation at a given age *shares* one probability. Vocabulary scores vary far more *between* children than a common probability allows. We therefore assume a Beta-Binomial distribution where each observation's probability is itself drawn from a Beta distribution, while (a) and (b) continue to hold within each observation.

---

The Binomial distribution describes the expected distribution of the number of 'yes' responses for a fixed number of items, assuming that (a) the probability of a 'yes' for each item is independent of the others (i.e., the items are exchangeable) and (b) that the probability is the same for each item. Clearly, it is unlikely that every child of the same age is equally likely to know each word on a checklist. 

 , so we relax the second assumption by allowing the probability itself to vary from observation to observation. This gives the counts a Beta-Binomial distribution, which is a Binomial distribution mixed over a Beta distribution for the success probability [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013, sec. 17.2; @qiaoBetaBinomialModelCount2025].

The item-exchangeability assumption is *not* relaxed by this construction: it survives inside the Binomial step, and it is false — words differ markedly in difficulty, which the checklist structure demonstrates directly (a model-free hypergeometric test against the three DSE checklists rejects it decisively). Two considerations establish that this does not threaten the estimates. First, under an item-response model with heterogeneous difficulties but equal discrimination, the total score is a *sufficient statistic* for a child's ability: the likelihood depends on the responses only through their sum, so modelling counts rather than individual words discards no information about ability, and difficulty heterogeneity can reach the model only through the distribution of the total. Second, that distributional effect is small where it matters. Heterogeneous difficulty makes the true count variance *lower* than Binomial — the opposite of the usual intuition — by an exact identity, $\sum_j p_j(1-p_j) = N\bar p(1-\bar p) - N\operatorname{Var}_j(p)$; but the Binomial kernel carries under 6% of total variance at every age in the fitted models, because between-child dispersion dominates it by one to two orders of magnitude, so even a 40% error in the kernel moves the total standard deviation by about 1%.



If every child of the same age were equally likely to know each word on the checklist, these counts would follow a Binomial distribution. Vocabulary scores vary more between children than that allows, so we let the chance itself vary from observation to observation, which gives the counts a Beta-Binomial distribution.

A Binomial likelihood would make two distinct assumptions, and it is worth separating them because the Beta-Binomial relaxes only one. The first is that, *given* an observation's success probability, the words of the inventory are exchangeable Bernoulli trials — every word equally likely to be known, so that the item list could be reordered without effect. The second is that there is no unmodelled heterogeneity between children, which fixes the variance at its mean and tends to *underdisperse* relative to real vocabulary data. To accommodate that extra-binomial variation we use a **Beta-Binomial** likelihood, in which the per-observation success probability is itself Beta-distributed [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013, sec. 17.2; @qiaoBetaBinomialModelCount2025]. With latent mean $p_i = p(z_i)$ and concentration $\kappa_i > 0$,

$$
y_i \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(N_{\text{trials}},\,\alpha_i,\,\beta_i\right),
\qquad
\alpha_i = p_i\,\kappa_i,
\qquad
\beta_i = (1-p_i)\,\kappa_i .
$$

---

For observation $i$ at age $x_i$ months we standardise age,

$$
z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{s_x},
$$

so that a one-unit change in $z$ corresponds to $s_x$ months (this scale differs by population and model — see the relevant appendix).

Smaller $\kappa_i$ implies greater dispersion of the observed counts at a given age; larger $\kappa_i$ approaches the Binomial. It is tempting to gloss this as "more between-child heterogeneity", and we avoid doing so: on a bounded inventory $\kappa$ is a property of the count distribution rather than a measurement of latent spread between children, and @sec-kappa sets out why the two do not track each other. Observations are assumed conditionally independent given the latent mean $p(z)$, the dispersion $\kappa(z)$, and the model parameters.

The item-exchangeability assumption is *not* relaxed by this construction: it survives inside the Binomial step, and it is false — words differ markedly in difficulty, which the checklist structure demonstrates directly (a model-free hypergeometric test against the three DSE checklists rejects it decisively). Two considerations establish that this does not threaten the estimates. First, under an item-response model with heterogeneous difficulties but equal discrimination, the total score is a *sufficient statistic* for a child's ability: the likelihood depends on the responses only through their sum, so modelling counts rather than individual words discards no information about ability, and difficulty heterogeneity can reach the model only through the distribution of the total. Second, that distributional effect is small where it matters. Heterogeneous difficulty makes the true count variance *lower* than Binomial — the opposite of the usual intuition — by an exact identity, $\sum_j p_j(1-p_j) = N\bar p(1-\bar p) - N\operatorname{Var}_j(p)$; but the Binomial kernel carries under 6% of total variance at every age in the fitted models, because between-child dispersion dominates it by one to two orders of magnitude, so even a 40% error in the kernel moves the total standard deviation by about 1%.

Sufficiency carries two conditions worth making explicit. It holds *given the administered item set*, because the ability-dependent term of the likelihood runs over the items actually put to the child; that is the principle behind the form-pooling and partial-administration rules in @sec-data, which is also why an administration missing a whole subscale is masked rather than rescaled onto the reference inventory. And it requires *equal discrimination* across items, exactly, which CDI items do not satisfy. Unequal discrimination leaves the variance budget above unchanged, since the identity holds for any set of per-item probabilities; but it means the count is not strictly sufficient, and the residual loss cannot be quantified from counts, because a statistic sufficient for ability is by construction uninformative about item parameters. It is an acknowledged approximation, bounded on the distributional axis and unmeasured on the other.

What item difficulty *does* affect is the interpretation of the production ratio $q$, which is a composition-weighted average over the words each child happens to know rather than an item-level probability (@sec-ratios), and the reading of $\kappa$ itself, discussed next.

### Age-varying dispersion {#sec-kappa}

Spoken vocabulary counts are more dispersed at older ages than at younger ones, and both experience and existing research lead us to expect that. We therefore let the conditional dispersion vary with age by modelling the concentration as a log-linear function of age above an asymptote,

$$
\kappa(z) = \kappa_{\min} + \exp\!\left(a_\kappa + b_\kappa z\right).
$$

The sign of $b_\kappa$ is **not constrained** in most current models. Every model with an empirically calibrated dispersion prior (VG01--VG04, VG09--VG13, VG15 and VG16) states the age term at two reference ages and derives $a_\kappa$ and $b_\kappa$ from them (see below), so the slope's sign is whatever the two anchors imply -- necessary because the fitted comprehension dispersion *rises* with age, which a negative-slope constraint cannot represent. Where the slope is negative, $\exp(a_\kappa + b_\kappa z)$ decreases, $\kappa(z)$ falls toward $\kappa_{\min}$, and dispersion increases with age before levelling off. The legacy parameterisation retained by VG05, VG07, VG08 and VG14 does impose that monotone decline, by setting $b_\kappa = -b_{\mathrm{mag}}$ with $b_{\mathrm{mag}} > 0$.

These are assumptions about the model's concentration parameter, and it is worth being explicit about what they are not. On a bounded inventory $\kappa$ **cannot** be read as latent between-child heterogeneity: a fitted decline in $\kappa$ is quantitatively consistent with latent spread that does not grow at all, and this is true even under perfect item exchangeability, so it is not a defect of the item model. Nor do these data yield a corrected estimate of how far children really diverge — a total score sufficient for ability carries no information about the item structure that separating the two would require. What the fitted $\kappa(z)$ licenses is a statement about the dispersion of observed counts at a given age, not a measurement of underlying heterogeneity.

## The mean trajectory {#sec-mean}

The latent mean trajectory is defined on the logit scale as a linear trend plus a zero-mean Gaussian process (GP) [@rasmussenGaussianProcessesMachine2008; @schulzTutorialGaussianProcess2018]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(z) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 z + g(z), \qquad
p(z) = \sigma\!\left(f(z)\right) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-f(z)}},\\
g(z) &= \eta\, g_{\mathrm{unit}}(z), \qquad
g_{\mathrm{unit}} \sim \mathcal{GP}\!\left(0,\, k(\cdot,\cdot)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The linear trend $\beta_0 + \beta_1 z$ carries the expected population trajectory; the GP $g$ captures smooth deviations from it. We use a zero mean function for $g$ because any non-zero mean would be confounded with the linear parameters — so positive $g(z)$ indicates faster-than-expected growth and negative $g(z)$ a slowdown or plateau, and under the posterior $g$ shrinks toward zero where data are sparse.

We use a unit-variance radial basis function (exponentiated-quadratic) kernel,

$$
k(z,z') = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z-z')^2}{2\ell^2}\right),
\qquad k(z,z) = 1,
$$

and factor out a separate amplitude $\eta > 0$. This cleanly separates two roles: the length-scale $\ell$ governs how quickly deviations vary with age (smoothness), while $\eta$ governs how large they are. The kernel is stationary (local smoothness is similar at, say, 36 and 72 months) and a universal approximator, which suits developmental trajectories whose precise shape is unknown.

### Interpretable slope anchors {#sec-anchors}

Rather than placing weakly interpretable priors directly on $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$, we parameterise the linear trend through the expected proportion of words at **two reference ages** $x_a < x_b$. With $z_a = (x_a - \bar{x})/s_x$ and $z_b = (x_b - \bar{x})/s_x$, and priors placed on $p_{x_a}$ and $p_{x_b}$,

$$
\beta_1 = \frac{\operatorname{logit}(p_{x_b}) - \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a})}{z_b - z_a},
\qquad
\beta_0 = \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a}) - \beta_1 z_a .
$$

This gives an interpretable baseline on the logit scale while the GP captures smooth departures. The reference ages and the priors on $p_{x_a}, p_{x_b}$ are **model-specific** (e.g. 24 and 84 months for the Down syndrome models; 12 and 26 months for the typically developing models) and are tabulated in each model's appendix.

### Levelling the trend above the high anchor {#sec-clamp}

The Down syndrome joint models evaluate the trajectory over 8–115 months while their anchors sit at 24 and 84, so about a quarter of the domain lies above the high anchor, where no prior constrains the trend. On the logit scale a line steep enough to climb between the anchors saturates over that distance. Extrapolated to 115 months, VG10's production-ratio mean alone reaches 0.993 — $P(\text{mean} > 0.99) = 0.90$ across the posterior — against a realised 0.842. The GP is then spent hauling the mean back, $-3.3$ logits at the top of the range, while sitting idle ($+0.08$) at 48 months where the data are.

We therefore level the trend off above the high anchor, replacing $z$ in the linear term with

$$
z_{\text{eff}} = z_b - \frac{1}{\beta}\operatorname{softplus}\!\big(\beta\,(z_b - z)\big),
\qquad \beta = \frac{50}{z_b - z_a},
$$

so the mean rises linearly below $z_b$ and flattens above it, leaving the GP free to carry departures rather than correct an asymptote. The same coordinate is used for the projection basis in @sec-gpanchor, so the two constraints stay consistent.

Three properties are deliberate. **The clamp is one-sided:** below the low anchor the line extrapolates accurately — VG10's production ratio at 12 months is 0.019 by extrapolation against 0.022 fitted — and clamping there would instead pin young-age values at the 24-month level, which is much worse. **The transition is smooth rather than a hard minimum:** $\min(z, z_b)$ is continuous but its derivative jumps at the anchor and the fitted curve inherits a visible elbow, which in the first VG10 refit made the spoken trajectory briefly non-monotone, falling from 428.6 words at 84.3 months to 426.6 at 85.6. **The softness is scale-free:** setting $\beta$ from the anchor span makes the largest departure from the hard-clamped form $\beta_1 \log 2 / \beta$, or 1.4% of the anchor span — about 0.8 months of age for the Down syndrome models — whatever the age standardisation.

The cost is that $p_{x_b}$ is no longer exactly the mean at the high anchor age, falling short by that same amount. Between the anchors the mean is untouched, so both anchor priors carry over unchanged.

This applies to the Down syndrome joint and signing models (VG05, VG07–VG10, VG14–VG16 and VG20, which inherits VG10's setting), set by `clamp_mean_above_hi_anchor` in each model definition. The typically developing models do not use it: their evaluation domains extend barely beyond their high anchors. The univariate Down syndrome baselines, VG01 and VG02, extrapolate the line across the full domain.

### HSGP approximation {#sec-hsgp}

Exact GP inference requires an $O(n^3)$ Cholesky factorisation. With several hundred observations per model this is feasible but costly inside MCMC, so we use the **Hilbert-space GP (HSGP)** approximation [@solinHilbertSpaceMethods2020; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022], a finite basis-function representation that generates $g_{\mathrm{unit}}$ from a unit-variance kernel and then rescales by $\eta$. Approximation quality depends on the basis size $m$ (accuracy vs cost), the boundary factor $c$ (the approximation domain, $c$ times the half-range of the standardised evaluation grid about its midpoint, must cover every point the basis is evaluated at), and the length-scale $\ell$ (shorter scales need more basis functions). We select $m$ and $c$ following PyMC's `approx_hsgp_hyperparams` recommendations for the specified range of $\ell$ [@abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022].

## Shared default priors {#sec-core-priors}

The following priors are held **constant across all models** (they are the shared defaults in `definitions.py`). Model-specific priors — the slope anchors $p_{x_a}, p_{x_b}$, and any random-effect, GP-anchor or association settings — are given in each appendix as deltas from this table.

| Parameter | Description | Prior |
|----|----------------|------------|
| $\ell_\text{unit}$ | Unit length-scale, mapped linearly to 6–18 months | $\mathrm{Beta}(3, 3)$ |
| $\eta$ | GP amplitude (logit scale) | $\mathrm{HalfNormal}(\sigma = 0.4)$ |
| $\kappa_{\min}$ | Minimum concentration (dispersion floor) | $\mathrm{LogNormal}(\mu = \log 5,\ \sigma = 0.6)$ |
| $a_\kappa$ | Log-scale intercept of $\kappa(z)$ | $\mathrm{Normal}(\mu = \log 8,\ \sigma = 1.0)$ |
| $b_{\mathrm{mag}}$ | Magnitude of the $\kappa$ decline rate ($b_\kappa = -b_{\mathrm{mag}}$) | $\mathrm{HalfNormal}(\sigma = 0.3)$ |

: Shared default prior distributions. {#tbl-core-priors}

**The three dispersion rows are the legacy parameterisation, and most models no longer use it.** Every model with an empirical dispersion calibration — VG01–VG04, VG09–VG13, VG15 and VG16 — states its dispersion prior at two reference *ages* instead, as a floor plus the age term at each anchor, from which $a_\kappa$ and $b_\kappa$ are derived:

$$
\kappa(a) = \kappa_{\min} + \exp\!\Big(\log e_{\text{young}} + \tfrac{a - a_{\text{young}}}{a_{\text{old}} - a_{\text{young}}}\,\big(\log e_{\text{old}} - \log e_{\text{young}}\big)\Big).
$$

Two things motivate it. A prior on $a_\kappa$ describes dispersion at the pool's *mean age*, so it silently changes meaning when the pool is resampled or filtered, where a prior at 24 months always means 24 months. And $b_{\mathrm{mag}} \ge 0$ forces dispersion to fall with age, which the comprehension outcomes reject — under the anchored form the sign is a consequence of the two anchors rather than a constraint. Anchor ages and medians are per model and are given in each appendix; the derivation and the calibration behind the numbers are in `docs/models/PRIORS.md`. The four that keep the table above — VG05, VG07, VG08 and VG14 — do so because their grouping structure differs from the pools the calibration covers, not because they were overlooked.

The length-scale is mapped from the unit interval onto a 6–18 month range, $\ell = \ell_{\min} + (\ell_{\max} - \ell_{\min})\,\ell_\text{unit}$, which favours changes over 6–18 month periods and offers better sampling geometry than a direct prior on the positive reals. The amplitude $\eta$ is constant on the logit scale but, through the logistic link, has its largest effect on counts near $p \approx 0.5$ (about 405 of 810 words) and least effect near the floor or ceiling — matching the expectation that there is least scope for variation when a child is just starting out or near the checklist limit.

## Extension mechanisms

The models differ only in which of the following mechanisms they switch on. Each maps directly onto a field (or flag) in `definitions.py`.

### Joint outcomes and production ratios {#sec-ratios}

The joint models estimate words **understood** and the conditional probability that an understood word is also produced. With $p_U(a) = \sigma(f_U(a))$ for understanding, define the **production ratio**

$$
q(a) = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understood}) = \sigma(h(a)),
\qquad
p_S(a) = p_U(a)\,q(a),
$$

where $f_U$ and $h$ each have their own linear-trend-plus-GP structure (@sec-mean). Because $q(a) \in (0,1)$, this enforces $p_S \le p_U$ by construction.

Two properties of $q$ belong here, at its definition, rather than in a later caveat, because both bear on every comparison the report makes with it.

**$q$ is a composition-weighted average, not an item-level probability.** The notation $P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understood})$ invites reading $q(a)$ as the probability that a given word is spoken once understood. It is not that. Words differ markedly in difficulty (@sec-betabinomial), and children at a given age understand different numbers of words and different *sets* of words, so $q(a)$ averages the per-word production probability over whatever vocabulary each contributing child happens to have. Two populations can differ in $q$ purely because their understood vocabularies are composed differently, with no difference in how readily any particular word is produced. The sufficiency argument in @sec-betabinomial is also the proof that this cannot be repaired within a sum-score model: a statistic sufficient for ability carries no information about item composition.

**A contrast at matched comprehension is not a contrast at matched age.** Where the report compares Down syndrome and typically-developing children at the same level of comprehension, the two groups are **8–13 months apart in age** at that matched level. A difference in $q$ read off such a comparison is therefore a difference between groups that are simultaneously unlike in age and in vocabulary composition, and neither can be held fixed while varying the other. Both qualifications apply wherever $q$ is reported.

The trivariate models add a **sign ratio**

$$
r(a) = P(\text{sign} \mid \text{understood}) = \sigma(g_{\text{sign}}(a)),
\qquad
p_{\text{Sign}}(a) = p_U(a)\,r(a) .
$$

The signed mean $g_{\text{sign}}$ is a three-anchor, piecewise logit-linear **tent** with young, peak and older reference levels, plus a GP for smooth departures. This allows a signing rise and decline without making the GP alone carry the entire shape. Each outcome retains its own age-varying dispersion (@sec-betabinomial, @sec-kappa).

For rows where understood and spoken counts are both available and satisfy $0 \le S_i \le U_i \le N$, the likelihood is a coherent factorisation,

$$
U_i \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(N,p_{U,i},\kappa_{U,i}), \qquad S_i\mid U_i \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(U_i,q_i,\kappa_{S,i}).
$$

The signing models use the parallel conditional likelihood $\mathrm{Sign}_i\mid U_i \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(U_i,r_i,\kappa_{\mathrm{Sign},i})$. Thus $q$ and $r$ are genuine conditional proportions for paired, logically nested counts rather than ratios imposed only on marginal means. When the understood count is unavailable, the child outcome remains usable through the marginal fallback $S_i\sim\mathrm{BetaBinomial}(N,p_{U,i}q_i,\kappa_{S,i})$ (and analogously for signing). A recorded child count greater than understood is retained through that fallback and counted as a source-data violation in the fit log rather than silently discarded. The same age-varying $\kappa_S$ is used for conditional and fallback rows, although it has different interpretations: conditional-row dispersion is variation in $q$, whereas fallback-row dispersion also absorbs unobserved variation in $p_U$. The fallback is therefore a pragmatic information-preserving approximation rather than a claim that the two dispersion processes are identical.

The size of that approximation is now known exactly rather than described. Binomial thinning collapses the paired factorisation to $S_i \mid \theta_{U},\theta_{S} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N, \theta_U\theta_S)$, so the true marginal of a fallback row is a Binomial mixed over the *product* of the two independent Beta variates. That product is not itself Beta, but both its moments are elementary, and comparing them against the fallback's cancels to a single condition: the true marginal is more dispersed than the fallback exactly when $q\kappa_S > \kappa_U$, with $p_U$ dropping out entirely, and the two variances are equal on the boundary. The fallback is therefore neither conservative nor anti-conservative as a structural matter — which way a given model errs is a question about its fitted concentrations. Three registered sensitivities bound it on VG10 and VG20: `paired-only` drops the fallback rows altogether, `fallback-dispersion` gives the branch its own concentration through a single signed scalar that nests the default at zero, and `marginal-moments` replaces the fallback's concentration with the one that matches the true marginal's first two moments. Posterior-predictive calibration is also reported separately for the two branches, since they are fitted by different distributions and differ systematically in age and study composition. In VG15, rows with the richer uk_02 four-cell table use the Dirichlet-Multinomial composition term instead of duplicate spoken and signed likelihood contributions; the understood likelihood remains because the four-cell model is conditional on its observed total.

The signing outcome is also harmonised before fitting. `uk_01` records sign-only words and cannot identify total signed vocabulary from the committed aggregate data, so its understood and spoken values are retained while its signing values are masked in the primary VG14, VG15 and VG17 analyses; an explicit sensitivity variant reintroduces it rather than pooling it silently with the comparable total-sign measures. The `uk_06` signing field was masked on the same principle from July 2026, its construct being unverified, and was reinstated in August once the source confirmed the instrument: the standard DSE checklists, whose second column is completed for a word the child *understands and signs*, ticked for imitated as well as spontaneous signs. That is a total sign count, and the committed data agrees — signed and spoken are each nested within understood on every uk_06 record, while their sum exceeds it on seven of eleven, which only overlapping per-word ticks can produce.

### Study and subject random intercepts {#sec-randomeffects}

To separate the population age curves from differences in study composition and from repeated measurements on the same child, we add random intercepts on the logit-scale predictors at the observation level. For a predictor $f_\bullet \in \{f_U, h, g_{\text{sign}}\}$,

$$
f_\bullet(z_i) \;\to\; f_\bullet(z_i) + \delta^{\text{study}}_{\bullet,\,s(i)} + \delta^{\text{subj}}_{\bullet,\,j(i)},
\qquad
\delta_\bullet \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \tau_\bullet),\ \ \tau^{\text{study}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(0.5),\ \ \tau^{\text{subj}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(1.5),
$$

implemented non-centred, where $s(i)$ and $j(i)$ index the study and subject of observation $i$. The two levels take different scales because they are on different scales in the data: fitting the same grouping structure outside the models puts the between-child standard deviation at 0.74–1.15 on the logit scale across the family, where between-study differences are around a third of that. Study intercepts absorb between-lab/between-study level differences; subject intercepts stop within-child repeated measurements being treated as independent. **The reported population curves set every random effect to zero**, so their interpretation is unchanged. Tiny studies can be trimmed before fitting (`min_study_observations`) to avoid near-unidentified intercepts.

The TD hierarchical models apply the same repeated-measures rule. VG11 and VG12 include a child intercept on their single outcome, and VG13 includes child intercepts on both $p_U$ and $q$. A fixed-seed sensitivity retains one randomly selected administration per study-specific child and disables the child effects, providing a cheaper check that conclusions do not depend on treating repeat administrations as additional independent children.

### Gaussian-process anchoring {#sec-gpanchor}

Once a random intercept and the linear/intercept term and the GP can each carry the global level, that level becomes redundant and sampling geometry degrades (a GP↔intercept ridge). We remove the redundancy by constraining each GP to pass through zero at a reference age $a_{\text{ref}}$ **for every posterior draw**,

$$
\tilde{g}(z) = \eta\left(g_{\mathrm{unit}}(z) - g_{\mathrm{unit}}(z_{\text{ref}})\right),
$$

so the level is owned solely by the linear/intercept term and the random effects, while the GP carries only the *shape* of departures around $a_{\text{ref}}$. The reference age $a_{\text{ref}}$ (`gp_anchor_age_months`) is model-specific.

### Within-understood sign–speech association {#sec-association}

For each understood word a child may sign it, speak it, both, or neither. The trivariate marginals $r$ and $q$ (@sec-ratios) leave the **overlap** unidentified; the joint model adds a single scalar **Plackett odds ratio** $\psi$ linking sign and speech within understood words via the copula $C(r, q; \psi)$:

$$
\pi_{\text{both}} = C(r, q; \psi),\quad
\pi_{\text{sign-only}} = r - \pi_{\text{both}},\quad
\pi_{\text{speak-only}} = q - \pi_{\text{both}},\quad
\pi_{\text{neither}} = 1 - r - q + \pi_{\text{both}} .
$$

$\psi = 1$ is independence ($\pi_{\text{both}} = r\,q$); $\psi > 1$ means a word is signed and spoken together more often than independence predicts. The four cells are fitted with a Dirichlet-Multinomial likelihood, identified from the four-cell cross-tabulation (the uk\_02 data; see @sec-data <!-- methods-data -->). The association yields a **data-identified total expressive vocabulary**

$$
p_{\text{any}}(a) = p_U(a)\left(r(a) + q(a) - \pi_{\text{both}}(a)\right),
$$

which sits below an independence-based upper bound whenever $\psi > 1$.

::: {.callout-important}
$\psi$ is a **single scalar**, identified from a small four-cell cross-tab, and is treated as **descriptive / exploratory** throughout this report. See @sec-sign-speech-association for the estimate, @sec-psi-by-study for how far the contributing sources disagree about it, and @sec-signing-limits for its scope and caveats.
:::

### Validation and publication gate {#sec-validation-gate}

Every fit writes `fit_manifest.json` immediately after preparing its analysis frame. The manifest records the exact model definition and priors, sampling configuration and seed, prepared-row counts by source and outcome, a SHA-256 hash of the prepared analysis frame, the Git revision and dirty state, Python/platform details, and installed package versions. This makes a fitted artefact traceable to the code and filtered data that produced it.

Validation is layered rather than reduced to a single fit statistic: prior predictive checks assess whether the priors generate plausible trajectories; posterior predictive checks compare replicated counts with observed age-stratified distributions; PSIS-LOO and leave-one-subject-out comparisons assess relative prediction where their assumptions are appropriate; source, prior and single-administration sensitivities test the main measurement and dependence decisions; and independent developmental norms are reserved for external calibration rather than prior tuning where possible. Reporting-quality (`rep` and `rep-lite`) runs are fail-closed: if any sampled parameter has $\hat R>1.01$, bulk or tail ESS below 400, or the convergence scan itself fails, diagnostic artefacts and a `CONVERGENCE_FAILED.txt` marker are retained but posterior summaries and report-generation stages do not run. Development and test fits remain explicitly provisional and report the same warnings without being treated as publication artefacts.
